title: Software Requirements Analysis
body:
[[Problem Recognition]]
[[Evaluation and Synthesis]]
[[Modeling]]
[[Specification]]
[[Review]]

The first phase of the [[SDLC]], and the one the rest of the course keeps pointing back at,
because a defect introduced here is the most expensive kind there is. Its job is to answer
"what does this system have to do", in writing, before anyone decides how.

**The five steps, in order:**

| Step | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| [[Problem Recognition]] | what is actually wrong, as opposed to what was asked for |
| [[Evaluation and Synthesis]] | what are the options, and which one do we take |
| [[Modeling]] | can we draw it so a person can check it |
| [[Specification]] | is it written down precisely enough to build and test against |
| [[Review]] | does the customer agree that this is what they meant |

The two kinds of requirement worth separating:

- **Functional**: what the system does. "The user can cancel an order before it ships."
- **Non-functional**: constraints on how it does it. Performance, reliability, security,
  usability. These are the ones that get left out, and they are the ones that force
  architecture, so leaving them out means the architecture gets chosen by accident.

A requirement is only finished if it is **testable**. "The system should be fast" cannot be
passed or failed; "a search returns within two seconds for a catalogue of 100,000 items" can.
This is the link to [[Project Success]], which is judged against the requirements: vague
requirements make success unmeasurable in both directions.

Sits inside [[System analysis]] as its written output.
